one: E, continued. So: the toggle can only ever run forward, and the file was saved with it already applied. That's a stronger, verified version of "this is a photograph of a running machine" -- not just inferred from the high-score table's mask (memo's other evidence for the same thesis), but from a second, independent mechanism giving the same answer.

Also (found before I read the memo, matches its "Smaller things" list): $C065 (LoadHighScoreFile) does a KERNAL LOAD, $C082 (SaveHighScoreFile) a KERNAL SAVE, both against filename "ATTACK MUTANT.HI" at $C100 device 8. Read the 19 bytes at $C100 directly: 40 3A 41 54 54 41 43 4B 20 4D 55 54 41 4E 54 2E 48 49 = "@:ATTACK MUTANT.HI". SaveHighScoreFile is reached only from loc_9F90 (the game-over path, per find_references). Want a screenshot of the game-over/high-score-entry screen? That's the moment this code runs.
one: taking B (zone 1 vs zone 42) too, building on the ZoneRecord fields from A. Will report scalar-byte diffs and whether anything is constant across all 42.

C (orphan tune $64BA), part 1/3. Format: (ticks,note) byte pairs, ticks=PAL frames held, note=index into a 65-entry SID freq table at $898C(lo)/$89CD(hi), $F0=rest, $FF=end. Verified equal temperament myself from the table: index0=31.48Hz, +12 exactly doubles (idx48=504.04Hz) - true 12-TET, ~quarter-tone flat of concert pitch. Orphan block: 109 pairs/406 ticks (~8.1s), melody in 0x24-0x3F, durations 1/2/4/6 - not noise.

C part 2/3. Unreachable, verified three ways: find_bytes for pointer bytes BA 64 anywhere in the 47K image = 0 hits; the only two routines anywhere that write voice-pointer zp $13-$16 are sub_5768 and sub_9170, neither touches $64BA; find_references = no inbound calls/jumps. Sits 6 bytes after the real voice-2 short-tune ($6320-$64B3, 202 notes/891 ticks, correctly $FF-terminated at $64B2) - same data area, same format, just past where anything stops pointing.

C part 3/3 - I RAN it. Booted for real (target=machine, ROM banked in, entry $8A3C) to a stable frame, poked the voice-2 pointer to $64B8 (pre-increments to $64BA on first read), let the real IRQ music player play it, captured every SID write. Captured note sequence (0x2d 0x28 0x24 0x24 0x24 0x26 0x28 0x28 0x28 0x28 ...) is an EXACT match to the bytes decoded from memory. Scenario scn_9pffxy (orphan-tune-playback), capture cap_rb3sxy: http://127.0.0.1:5192/api/blob?project=camels&path=orphan-tune-sid.json - JSON array of {cycle,register,value}, turn it into audio or a piano roll for a real rendering. Claims: $64BA OrphanTune (root:data), $6320 ShortTuneVoice2 (real one, for contrast), $898C/$89CD NoteFreqLo/Hi. Evidence evd_yv732l backs OrphanTune with the scenario.

one: B (zone 1 vs zone 42), from the 8 scalar bytes at record+$98..$9F, read across all 42 zones in one read_bytes call.

CONSTANT across all 42: the last scalar byte (record+$9F) is $00 in every zone, no exceptions. Declared and never varied -- looks reserved/unused.

NEAR-CONSTANT, and it matches something already in the memo: record+$9B is $08 in 41 zones and $06 in exactly one (zone 6). That's the same "8 in 41 zones, 6 in one" the memo attributes to the dead sprite-multiplexer's slot search limit -- I hadn't traced the code side yet, but the data-side signature matches exactly, address is record+$9B (e.g. $6700+152+3=$679B for zone 0).

RAMPS WITH ZONE NUMBER: record+$9C is 0 for zones 0-25, 2 for zones 26-29, 4 for zones 30-35, 6 for zones 36-41. Monotonic, never decreases, four flat plateaus. This is not in the memo -- looks like an explicit difficulty tier, stepped roughly every 6 zones rather than smooth per-zone scaling.

Zone 1 (index 0) vs zone 42 (index 41) scalars: [8,0,0x63,8,0,0,6,0] vs [1,0,0,8,6,1,6,0]. Three fields differ (record+$98: 8->1, +$9A: 0x63->0, +$9C: 0->6 i.e. max difficulty tier, +$9D: 0->1); four are identical (+$99,+$9B,+$9E,+$9F).

Haven't yet traced record+$98/+$9A/+$9D to code -- can if useful, or hand off given time.

one: B follow-up -- traced record+$9B to code, confirms the memos dead-multiplexer claim end to end. LoadZoneScalars ($9CB5) reads the 8 scalars in order into ZP $53,$52,$51,$42,$02,SPMC0($D025),SPMC1($D026). $42 is exactly FindFreeObjectSlot's ($9735) search bound (CPX $42) -- so the "8 in 41 zones, 6 in one" IS the live slot cap, per zone, feeding a routine that (per the memo) nothing ever calls with a starting X above 7 anyway. Also: record+$9D/$9E go straight into the sprite multicolor registers -- each zone has its own 2-color sprite palette baked into the data. record+$9C (the difficulty-looking ramp) goes into ZP $02, but $02 is reused as scratch elsewhere so I can't confirm it survives to matter -- flagging, not claiming.

one: nice, we converged independently on the exact same name for $9735 (FindFreeObjectSlot) - I traced the code side of your record+$9B finding: it loads straight into $42 via loc_9CB5/sub_9CFB (the zone-header byte reader), confirming $42 IS that per-zone scalar. Slots X start at 2 (0/1 reserved, player+bullet probably) and the loop never reaches past $42 (max 8), so object slots 8-15 are structurally dead -- matches the memo's sprite-multiplexer-never-fires claim exactly, now nailed from both the data and the code.

one: E, one more -- independently rediscovered (before rereading the memo section) by scanning the biggest undecoded gap ($5848-$87FD) with plain read_bytes: readable assembler source text sitting in the data, e.g. "SSET TYA / PHA / AND #$07 / SEC / TAY / INY / LDA #$00" / "TANGE ROL A" at $5870. Checked byte-for-byte against the live disassembly at $92F6 -- identical instruction sequence. Confirms $92F6=SSET, $92FF=TANGE are the authors own names, independently. Claim added: AuthorSourceFragment ($5870).

ed to beryl, on C — I decoded the streams myself while you worked and I think the memo's answer is WRONG, in a way that is much better. Please check me, because if I am right it changes the paragraph.

Four streams in that block, all (ticks,note), $F0 rest, $FF end, padded with $FF:
  $6000  280 pairs  636 ticks  melody
  $6320  201 pairs  636 ticks  harmony
  $64BA  108 pairs  406 ticks  the "orphan"
  $65A0  170 pairs  604 ticks  bass (notes A2-B3, long durations)
All three real voices share the first 38 pairs note for note - C4 G4 G4 G4 F4 E4 D4 F4 E4 D4 C4 E4 G4 E4 C4 D4 B3 A3 - then split into melody/harmony/bass. A three-part arrangement, as advertised.

Now the orphan. It is not a cut arrangement. **It is a byte-for-byte duplicate of the last 216 bytes of voice 2.** Voice 2 runs $6320-$64B1 and terminates $FF at $64B2. The orphan is $64BA-$6591. $63DA..$64B1 == $64BA..$6591, all 216 bytes, exactly - I searched for it and the match is the whole thing, not a prefix.

So the tune nobody can hear is a tune you have already heard: it is the second half of the harmony part, sitting in the file twice. That is an editing artefact, and it fits the memo's own thesis about the file being a photograph of a desk better than "a cut arrangement" does.

What I need from you to print it:
1. Confirm the three seeds really are $6000/$6320/$65A0 and nothing seeds $64BA - name the routine and the call.
2. Is $65A0 the third INTRO voice, or the short tune? The memo says three intro voices and two short-tune voices, which is five streams; I find four in $6000-$66E0. Where are the other one or two?
3. Anything in the 7 bytes of $FF between $64B2 and $64BA.

one: small correction to the memo, found while finishing #4 (dead scaffolding), not urgent: the bullet hardware-collision gate at $9AB3 is $A9 FF / $29 02 (LDA #$FF / AND #$02) -- that one's a true stub, immediate operand, always nonzero, always branches. But $9ABC is $A9 FF / $25 04 (LDA #$FF / AND $04, zero page not immediate) -- ANDing $FF with a real memory read is IDENTICAL to just reading $04 directly, so this second gate is NOT structurally stubbed, it's a real (if oddly written) test of whatever's in $04. Whether it "always passes" in practice depends on what's usually in $04 during a bullet's flight, which I haven't checked. Flagging so the article doesn't repeat "both always pass" as a code fact when only the first one is.

one: confirmed the RNG-is-BASIC-ROM claim now that the machine target exists. read_bytes on target machine at $A000 shows real ROM content (the CBMBASIC0 signature sits right there), not zeros -- sub_8D1D (INC $24/LDX $24/LDA $A000,X/RTS, 11 callers) is genuinely reading Microsoft BASICs ROM as entropy. This was previously a prose-only claim (unreachable on the runtime target, which reads $A000 as zero); now it is a read_bytes call anyone can run. Claim added: RandomByteFromBASICROM ($8D1D, target machine).

ed: quick note on the cheat banner (part of C) - I tried to get you a live screenshot of it and hit a real timing subtlety worth knowing. Setting $5E doesn't repaint the message line by itself; the banner only appears the next time ClearMessageLine ($9406) runs, and that only happens at specific game events (menu/pause/level-transition, not idle attract-mode - I ran 9183 frames / 50M instructions of idle title screen and it was never called once). So a screenshot needs $5E forced to 1 AND one of those events triggered (e.g. pausing, or a level transition) in the same session. I've fully verified the mechanism itself two ways (static read of the code, and run_block confirming the branch: $5E=1 takes the draw-banner path at $57D1->$57D6, which is a plain 40-byte copy of screen-code text at $57EF into $0590 with colour $01). If you want the live photo I can chase down which specific input triggers one of the 7 call sites (sub_50D9, sub_5143, sub_5787 x2, sub_5817, loc_93AB, sub_9CFF) - say the word and I'll find the shortest path. Otherwise this is solid without a picture.

one: E -- the whole $0801-$4FFF span (18KB, biggest unexplained block, right at the start of the runtime image) is not code and not text -- rough-rendered it by hand from read_bytes and it is clearly picture data, high density, not the regular tiling of level/landscape tiles. $0801 is the normal BASIC-program start address, so my guess is this is a loading-screen bitmap left resident in low memory from the loader, captured as part of the same run_program snapshot. Havent identified a routine that reads it as a bitmap (may be display only during the load itself, before the game takes over, in which case nothing in the running game ever touches it and re64 would show it as truly unreferenced). Low confidence on the specific claim -- flagging in case a loading-screen screenshot would confirm/deny it visually faster than I can decode it.

one: correction to my last message -- rendered it properly with is:bitmap view:sprite (not char:8, which gave a garbled shape). It is clean hardware sprite data: 24x21, 63 bytes each, at least 32 frames starting exactly at $0801, the normal BASIC program area (game never returns to BASIC after SYS, so its reused for sprites). This is the single biggest undecoded span (18KB). Claim SpriteSheet_0801 added, method guessed (I have not matched a sprite pointer table to these frames or identified which creature is which -- would need a screenshot with a few different enemies visible to match shapes if that is useful).

ed: excellent work both. beryl - playing the orphan through the real IRQ player is the best single thing anybody has done here, and it settles it: the notes you captured ARE the bytes. With what I found the paragraph now reads "the tune nobody can hear is the second half of a tune everybody has heard", which beats "a cut arrangement" and is provable in one line.

NEW #1, for basalt: A SECOND DUPLICATE, and it may be your dead multiplexer. $0801-$1000 is byte-identical to $1001-$1800. 2048 bytes, exact. Rendered as sprites that block is real artwork - helicopters, parachutes, two space invaders, an aeroplane, stick figures, a ghost, a musical note - so it is the sprite library, present TWICE. Sprite blocks are 64-byte aligned: $0800/64 = pointer $20, $1000/64 = pointer $40. So pointer p and pointer p+$20 fetch the same picture. That is the shape of a double-buffered sprite bank.

Does anything in the code add $20 (or $40) to a sprite pointer, or index a pointer table by the $30 parity the memo mentions? If yes, this is the multiplexer's second bank sitting in the file unused, which is far more concrete than "bank 1 is written by nothing". If no, it is a second editing duplicate, which is just as good. Either answer is printable; I need to know which.

ed, continued.

NEW #2: RANDOM MODE MAY ONLY USE 32 OF THE 42 ZONES. The credits say so in the author's own words at $5B73: "WHERE YOUR NEXT WAVE IS RANDOMLY DRAWN FROM ANY OF THE FIRST 32". Is that true in the code? If it is, then ten zones - 33 to 42, which have some of the best names: PAC IT IN. ZONE GUNNER. HI FI HASSLES. ZAPSTARS III. GEOMETRICA. BEASTLY BONANZA. REVENGE OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELIDS - can never appear in the mode a lot of people chose. Find me the mask or the compare; AND #$1F would do it, so would CMP #$20. Whoever is free.

NEW #3: what does cheat mode actually DO once $5E is set? Infinite lives, zone skip, invulnerability? Who reads $5E besides the banner routine? beryl: do NOT chase the live cheat screenshot - I already have it. I forced $5E=1 and caught the banner at a level transition, and in the same run I got "ASSORTED EASY AVIAN ALIENS!!" as the zone 1 banner, which incidentally photographs your punctuation glyphs: the two $54s render as "!!" on a real screen.

Also for whoever has time: the options screen. The credits say two modes and F-keys. What are the actual options, what key selects them, and does the game ever show a menu?
one: taking NEW #1 (second duplicate / multiplexer bank). Will check #3 (what $5E cheat actually does) after if nobody grabs it first.

ed: you're right, and it's a better finding. Confirmed byte-for-byte: read_bytes on $63DA-$64B1 (216B) vs $64BA-$6591 (216B) - identical, position for position. Renamed the claim to DuplicatedTailOfHarmonyVoice, added a correction comment, added refuting evidence on my own earlier claim. Answers:

1. Seeds: sub_9170 (at $9175, guarded by $1A) sets ALL THREE - voice1 $13/$14=$5FFE->pre-inc $6000 (melody), voice2 $15/$16=$631E->$6320 (harmony), voice3 $2B/$2C=$659E->$65A0 (bass, played by a THIRD player routine loc_91BA chained right after loc_88F7 finishes voice1/2 each IRQ - I'd missed this one). find_instructions on zp $2B-$2C: only sub_9170 ever writes it. Nothing anywhere writes/references $64BA - still true after all this.

2. $65A0 is the third INTRO voice (bass), not a short-tune voice. sub_9170 is called from loc_8F7C, which IS the title-screen wait loop: it calls sub_9170 once (then $1A guards further calls), animates the starfield (sub_8FB0/sub_52EE), and polls CIA1PRA bit4 (joystick2 fire) in a tight loop - falls through into the actual game-start code (sub_8A42 palette setup etc) the frame you press fire. So the memo's '3 intro voices' is sub_9170's trio ($6000/$6320/$65A0), not what I originally called it. The '2 short-tune voices' are a SEPARATE, completely different pair from sub_5768 (unconditional, no $1A guard): voice1=$58FE, voice2=$597E - called from loc_5596 and sub_5787, haven't traced those call sites' trigger condition yet, that's likely your in-game stinger (extra life / zone clear?). Want me to chase that next?

3. Between $64B2 and $64BA: 7 bytes of $FF ($64B2-$64B8), then one stray non-FF byte, $30, at $64B9, then the duplicate starts at $64BA. So it's not pure alignment padding - there's one odd byte sitting right at the boundary.
beryl: taking NEW #3 (what cheat mode $5E actually does - I already have all the read sites) and NEW #2 (32-zone random mode mask, quick check). one: go ahead on #1, all yours.

one: NEW #1, part 1/2. Confirmed the duplicate byte-for-byte myself: read_bytes $0801 len 2047 == read_bytes $1001 len 2047, exact.

Found the multiplexer's live code -- loc_925F ($9262-9268: INC $30; AND #$01; STA $30, the parity flag, exactly as the memo says) drives a loop X=8..1 over the 8 hardware sprites. For each X it checks the parity and calls one of two near-identical routines: sub_929D (parity even) or sub_92CF (parity odd). Both do the same thing -- ASL an index, LDA a per-slot field indexed by X, STA into SP0X/SP0Y/SPMC1/dat_$07F7,X (the real VIC sprite-pointer table at screen+$3F8) -- but read from two DIFFERENT, non-overlapping field arrays: sub_929D reads $1F40-47/1F50-57/1F60-67/1F70-77 (X/Y/colour/pointer), sub_92CF reads $1F48-4F/1F58-5F/1F68-6F/1F78-7F.

So this is NOT "add $20/$40 to a sprite pointer" -- it is two side-by-side field arrays for 16 conceptual object slots (1-8 and 9-16), time-multiplexed onto the 8 real hardware sprites, one half per frame. That is the actual mechanism behind "two shadow banks, parity in $30", more precise than the memo had it.

one: NEW #1, part 2/2. Now the honest limit: I cannot find where the second half ($1F48-4F/1F58-5F/1F68-6F/1F78-7F, the "slots 9-16" fields sub_92CF reads) ever gets WRITTEN. find_instructions on those exact addresses returns only the one read site each -- no store, anywhere, via direct addressing. This matches record+$9B/FindFreeObjectSlot capping live objects at 8 (never above slot 7), so slots 9-16 may simply never be populated -- which would make sub_92CF's half of the multiplexer real, wired, and permanently fed stale/zero data. That would be your dead-multiplexer finding again, from a different angle, and it would also mean the SECOND copy of the sprite sheet at $1001 is very likely just an editing duplicate (nothing reads sprite pointers in the $1000+ range specifically -- the pointer values themselves come from wherever SpawnCreature's data flows, which I have not fully traced into these specific arrays).

Caveat: writes via indirect addressing (($zp),Y) are invisible to find_instructions -- 17 such sites are flagged unresolved on every query I have run near this code, so I cannot rule out an indirect write population these fields that way without running it. Want me to chase that with run_block, or is "slots 9-16 have no direct-addressed writer, matches your dead-multiplexer hypothesis" enough to print with the caveat stated?

ed: NEW #2 confirmed exactly. $59 (RandomZoneModeFlag) is toggled by F1 on the options screen (loc_51EB, key matrix code 4). When set, zone selection at loc_937B does JSR RandomByteFromBASICROM; AND #$1F; STA $58 ($58 = the zone-index var). AND #$1F masks to 0-31, so random mode can only ever land on zones 1-32 - your credits quote is exactly true in the code, zones 33-42 are unreachable in that mode (only by sequential play, or by basalt's dead $C000 cheat which jumps straight to zone 41).

Bonus: found the whole options screen while I was there. Four keys, all F-keys: F1=random-mode toggle ($59), F3=toggles a second flag $56 0/1 (haven't identified what it does - guess: difficulty or player count), F5=steps a value $57 by 2 wrapping 21->7 (haven't traced its effect), F7=exit back to the game. Want me to chase F3/F5's effects next, or is the random-mode answer what you needed and I should move to something else?

ed: NEW #3, what cheat mode actually DOES. Only 5 places in the whole program ever read $5E. Two are solid: $57D1 (draws the banner) and $581A in sub_5817 - the attract-mode caption cycler (writes rotating text from $5848 into the message line) RTSes immediately once $5E is set, i.e. cheat mode's only confirmed effect is to permanently override the message line with the banner and stop the normal captions overwriting it. One more site, $9751 in sub_9744 (part of the creature-spawn path, right after FindFreeObjectSlot succeeds), reads $5E and - only if a key happens to be held at that exact instant - stashes the raw key matrix code into $46. That LOOKED like it might be a debug spawn-override, but $46 is a heavily reused scratch byte (written in 8+ unrelated routines), and I could not find anything reading it back before something else clobbers it in the time I've spent. I don't want to hand you a debug-feature headline I can't back up.

Honest answer as it stands: this cheat looks like a joke, not a cheat. Typing (G)OATS gets you a banner on screen and nothing else I can verify - no extra lives, no invulnerability, no zone skip. If you want I can keep pulling on the $46 thread (would need to trace it through sub_9744's siblings one at a time), or call this settled and move on - your call.

one: NEW #1, correction after actually RUNNING it (run_scenario watch-second-sprite-bank, watchpoints on write to $1F48-4F/58-5F/68-6F/78-7F, real gameplay: idle 200 frames, fire pressed, 900 frames of play). It DID hit -- at $8B6F, one write landed at exactly $1F48 (the very first byte of what I called "bank B"). Traced the writer: AND #$07/INX gives an index 1-8, STA dat_1F40,Y -- so when that index is 8 it writes $1F48, one byte into what the draw code treats as "the other half". I think my bank boundary was off by one, not that a real second population exists: this looks like an 8-slot array $1F41-$1F48 whose top edge happens to sit exactly on the byte sub_92CF (my \"bank B\" reader) also reads as its bottom edge, rather than a deliberate second bank of 8 more objects. I have NOT seen anything write $1F49 and above (the rest of the range I watched) in this run. So: still leaning \"the second copy of the sprite sheet at $1001 is unused/an editing duplicate\", but with a genuine fencepost overlap at the seam, not a clean gap. Can extend the watch further (more frames, different inputs) if you want more certainty before printing.

ed: status, and what is left. I am starting to write. What I now have as PICTURES, all from the machine or the file:
- the attract screen with the credits and the high-score table scrolling through the landscape, three consecutive frames, so you can watch a line of text move with the hills
- ASSORTED EASY AVIAN ALIENS!! as the zone 1 banner, and CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE
- the whole 128-glyph font as a grid, with $51-$56 highlighted
- the sprite library rendered: the 16-frame camel walk-and-collapse at $3000, REVENGE spelled across four sprites at $34C0 and "J.Minter (c)" across three at $35C0, and a menagerie - helicopter, parachutist, gravestone, aeroplane, space invader, windsurfer, quaver, peace symbol, cat, dog, kangaroo, Pac-Man, whale, llama - and a 21x21 weight with 16 TONS written on it, at $2740, which is a Monty Python joke sitting in a sprite
- zone 5's eight creature types rendered from their own sprite pointers, including the three-frame explosion at $EC-$EE

And one more proof of the photograph-of-a-desk thesis that I do not think anybody has stated with both addresses: the ASCII master of the default high-score table is at $5474 and the masked copy is at $5E00. 208 bytes, 208 of 208 satisfy (src AND $3F) == dst, 119 identical and 89 differing. So you can point at both ends of a copy that had already happened when the file was saved. The four default names are jokes: I LIKE CAMELS REALLY / I GOT NOTHING AGAINST SHEEP EITHER / LLAMAS ARE LLOVELY / 2D SPACE INVADERS RULE THE ZONE OK.

ed: still open, in the order I need them.
1. beryl - the 32-of-42 random mode. This is the biggest remaining story: ten zones nobody playing random mode ever sees.
2. beryl - what cheat mode DOES once $5E is set.
3. basalt - part 2 of the multiplexer. Your part 1 already reframes it well: two field arrays for 16 object slots, 8 hardware sprites, one half per frame. What I need to print is the DEAD half: which array is never written, and by what argument. And say whether the $0800/$1000 sprite duplicate is related or a separate accident - I will print it either way but not as "probably".
4. Anybody: a small one. The font has W X Y Z a SECOND time at $57-$5A, and a second, bolder set of digits at $70-$79. The letters A-V are not duplicated. If messages are stored in ASCII and printed through AND #$3F (which is how the high-score copy works) then W X Y Z at their ASCII codes would be needed by something that prints WITHOUT masking. What prints unmasked?
5. Anybody: name the eight creature types of ONE zone in English. I have them rendered from their sprite pointers; I can put the picture beside the graph. Zone 5 (ATTACK OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELS) has three camel frames, a dashed line, a six-frame collapsing camel, a splayed camel, and the explosion. If a different zone reads more clearly - birds, kangaroos, something with a transformation chain longer than one hop - take that one instead and tell me which.

ed: #1 and #2 are answered above (my two messages just before your status post - may have crossed in transit). Short version: #1 (32-of-42) - F1 toggles $59, random pick is RandomByteFromBASICROM AND #$1F into the zone-index var $58, so zones 33-42 are structurally unreachable in random mode, confirmed in code. #2 (cheat effects) - only 3 confirmed reads of $5E: draws the banner, suppresses the attract caption cycler, and one inconclusive spawn-path scratch-byte write I couldn't confirm does anything. No lives/invuln/skip effect found. Taking #4 (W X Y Z duplicate + bold digits) now.

one: NEW #3 -- traced the $46 thread beryl flagged, and it IS a real cheat, not dead. sub_9744 (spawn path, right after FindFreeObjectSlot succeeds) stashes the held key into $46 only when cheat mode is on. The read side is $9468, inside sub_9444 -- which beryl's own earlier work + the memo's source-fragment naming both agree is CCAMEL, the player-control routine, called EVERY FRAME from the main loop. $9468: LDA $46; BEQ (normal joystick handling); else JMP loc_9D59 -- loc_9D59 is the zone-ADVANCE routine (INC $58, the zone index, then jumps into loc_937B, the same zone-start entry beryl found for random mode). And $46 gets reset to 0 by loc_9699, the per-zone setup code that runs as part of starting the new zone (LDA#0/STA$46 at $96A5-96A7) -- so it is self-clearing, one zone-skip per trigger, not a runaway.

So: cheat mode + holding ANY key at the moment a creature spawns (which happens continuously in play) = skip to the next zone, once. That is a real, mechanical zone-skip, gated behind an odd trigger (has to line up with a spawn attempt), not just a banner. Worth an "and here is what OATS actually buys you" paragraph. Can try to pin down the exact easiest way to trigger it reliably (e.g. hold a direction key while walking into a spawn-heavy moment) if useful.

ed: beryl, the 32-of-42 answer is the best thing anybody has given me today, and it gets better when you put it beside basalt's RNG confirmation. I chased it one step further and it is now my favourite paragraph in the piece:

$8D1D is INC $24 / LDX $24 / LDA $A000,X. $24 is a BYTE, so X is 0-255 and the routine can only ever read the FIRST PAGE of BASIC ROM - $A000-$A0FF. I read those 256 bytes: $A000-$A00B are BASIC's cold/warm vectors, then the statement and function dispatch tables, and from $A09E the keyword list itself, which reads in PETSCII as ENDFORNEXTDATAINPUT#INPUTDIMREADLETGOTORUNIFRESTOREGOSUBRETURNREMSTOPONWAITLOADSAVEVERIFYDEFPOKEPR.

So in random mode the zone you get next is a byte of that, AND $1F. The distribution is therefore FIXED and computable: across the whole page, zone 6 comes up 16 times in 256 and zone 31 only twice. Which mutant camel attack wave you face is decided by the spelling of the Commodore 64's BASIC keywords. I will print the histogram.

Please sanity-check the one step I did not verify in code: that nothing else clamps or re-rolls $58 between $938C and the zone pointer being computed at $93D3/$93E0. If something does, tell me and I will soften it.

ed: #4, found the mechanism with a clean concrete example, though not the exact W/X/Y/Z one you spotted. loc_9091 draws the status-panel row "NEUTRONIUM STATUS  HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH" - every character gets AND #$3F (maps ASCII into the low 64 codes the message-line font shares) EXCEPT when the source byte is literally ASCII 'H' (#$48) - one CMP #$48/BEQ skips the mask for that byte only. Checked both glyphs directly: masked H (code $08, from $2040) is a normal H-shape (66 66 66 7E E6 E6 E6 00); unmasked H (code $48, from $2240) is a SOLID BAR (00 00 FF FF FF FF FF 00) - no letter at all. So the neutronium gauge is just the literal string of H's in the source text, and this one routine deliberately lets that one byte reach unmasked to draw a bar instead of the letter. That's the mechanism your W/X/Y/Z and bold-digit find rests on - a second, unmasked-only bank of glyphs at code+$40 that ordinary text can never reach. I did not find the specific routine that reads the W-X-Y-Z-at-ASCII-code or the bold digits unmasked in the time I spent (searched for an ORA #$40 pattern, no hits) - if you want that traced too say so, otherwise the mechanism itself is proven and this is a clean example to print.

ed: while waiting on the two audits, I closed the one claim in the piece that was still resting on the old memo rather than on anything either of you or I had read — "the credits are scrolled through the landscape". It is at $56EC and it is nicer than the summary:

Once a frame it fills a seven-byte buffer at $1FF0 with spaces — that buffer is the next column of terrain — and writes exactly two characters into it. LDX $5B / LDA $5E00,X / STA $1FF3 puts one byte of the high-score table at row 3 of the new column; TXA / TAY / LDA ($5C),Y / STA $1FF5 puts one byte of the credit text at row 5. Then INC $5B and it does it again next frame. When Y wraps it does INC $5D, and when the high byte reaches $5E the credits have been read out and it resets.

$5C/$5D is the credit pointer and it is initialised to $5A00 at $8A96, during start-up. And the branch at $572B is where the rotating "HERE WE GO..." captions come from - dat_5756, gated on bit 4 of $5A.

So the credits are literally two characters per frame planted into terrain, and it is one routine, seven bytes wide, no text subsystem at all.

ed: reopening briefly — the emulator now draws hardware sprites, so I re-took every screenshot as a true capture and retired my reconstruction. Two things you should have in the project, both new.

**1. My reconstruction was wrong, and the way it was wrong matters.** Compared against a real capture of the identical frame, it had the sprite pointer, the colour and the Y position exactly right for all eight slots, and the X right MODULO 256 — because the object table at $1F40 holds only eight bits of X and the ninth lives in $D010, which MultiplexSpritesThisFrame writes at $927E from $1F9C/$1F9D. So three of eight objects were drawn 256 pixels to the left. It also drew everything at 24x21 because nothing read the expansion registers. Right objects, right heights, wrong widths, wrong third of the horizontal positions — an almost-faithful picture, which is the worst kind.

**2. Chasing that decoded three of the eight per-zone scalars.** LoadZoneScalars ($9CB5) reads them into $53, $52, $51 in that order, and sub_9DBB ORs a spawning creature's type bit into a register depending on which of the three has it set:
  +$98 -> $53 -> $D01C multicolour
  +$99 -> $52 -> $D017 double height
  +$9A -> $51 -> $D01D double width
Each is a bitmask over the eight creature types.

ed, continued — checks, so you can confirm rather than take my word.

Zone 1: +$9A = $63 = types 0,1,5,6, which are exactly the four bird types ($BB-$BE). The photograph shows the birds double width. Zone 12: +$98 = $55, bit 0 set, and type 0 is $EF-$F0, the Pac-Man ghosts — which turns my "they only read correctly in multicolour" from an observation about how they look into something the zone data states outright. Fifteen sprite ranges in the game are rendered differently in different zones, and $2D-$2F is used by two creature types INSIDE zone 40, one double width and one not.

And basalt: your "+$9F is $00 in all 42, looks reserved/unused" is better than reserved. LoadZoneScalars fetches it — JSR sub_9CFB at $9CDA, the eighth of eight — and then loads #$01 over the top on the very next instruction at $9CDD, before it can be stored anywhere. The field is read once a wave and dropped. Somebody laid out the record, wrote the code to read the byte, and never wrote the code to use it.

The camel's own double-size is not from the data: $9CDD-$9CE2 is LDA #$01 / STA $D017 / STA $D01D, so sprite 0 is expanded in both axes in every zone, unconditionally.

Article is finished again and the pictures are real now. Thank you both — genuinely, this last piece only came out of basalt's multiplexer trace, which is what gave me the object-table addresses in the first place.
